extracted.intended_audience: agency policymakers and lawyers; social media managers for government agencies; First Amendment scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and doctrinal criteria for how federal agencies should moderate public comments on agency-sponsored social media, balancing First Amendment protections, tort law, statutory immunity, and practical/policy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public concern / topicality (public concern standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that express a political, social, community concern, or address topics of general interest to the public meet the public concern standard (see San Diego v. Roe; Connick v. Myers; Bartnicki v. Vopper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements concerning public figures or matters of public concern are likely to be protected speech; agencies should treat topical comments as subject to stronger First Amendment protection when evaluating removal or moderation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyberstalking and cyberharassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyberstalking generally involves a credible threat or repeated conduct via electronic communications; cyberharassment does not require a credible threat. Many states prosecute these behaviors under stalking/harassment laws or specific cyberstalking statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that approach a crime, even a non-federal crime, should be removed, especially if a victim requests it. Cyberstalking/harassment on agency social media may be easier to spot (repeated, directed comments). Agencies may be more proactive in patrolling for actual crimes and remove such speech preemptively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation / libel / slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation requires a false and defamatory statement communicated to a third party, publisher negligence, and damages; libel is permanent defamation (written), slander is oral. Public-figure plaintiffs must show actual malice (knowing falsity or reckless disregard for truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies sometimes enjoin speech that falls outside the narrow boundaries of defamation; the falsity element is hard to prove and hard to identify (opinions and many accusations are excluded). Preemptive removal of potentially libelous comments may violate free speech; decisions should be contextual and mindful of heightened standards for public figures. The Telecommunications Act (§ 230) may insulate agencies from liability for third-party speech, reducing the need for overbroad removals.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements of fact (general doctrine and exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the most part the First Amendment shields those who make false statements even intentionally; false ideas or false facts are often tolerated (with exceptions like commercial fraud).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are ill-advised to adopt categorical bans on 'false' comments (HHS’s blanket prohibition is problematic and chills speech). Better practice: leave false statements posted and respond publicly. Narrow exception: where the agency's mission and the falsehood have a credible potential to cause harm (e.g., public health misinformation about vaccines, disease spread, efficacy of medicines), the agency may have a substantial interest that could justify refusing to post or removing such false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial speech and advertisement-like posts
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial speech is likely to be considered off-topic on agency social media sites, but restrictions on commercial speech are governed by a more lenient First Amendment standard (Central Hudson and related cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial statements that function as advertisements (e.g., housing ads) can be treated differently and may be removed if they violate statutory prohibitions (e.g., Fair Housing Act § 804 forbids advertising that indicates preference or discrimination). Agencies should apply the appropriate commercial-speech analysis rather than treating all commercial posts identically to political speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminatory statements in statutory contexts (Fair Housing example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements on an agency’s site that amount to illegal advertisements or classified ads (e.g., 'apartment available willing to rent whites only') violate statutory prohibitions like Section 804 of the Fair Housing Act and can be removed and prosecuted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, non-commercial advocacy of repeal, critique, or ideological objection to a statute (even if discriminatory in sentiment) generally remains protected unless it meets the Brandenburg incitement test (intent, imminent lawless action, likely effect). Agencies should distinguish illegal commercial/classified postings from protected ideological advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of offensive, hyperbolic, or absurd statements about private individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive, hyperbolic, or ludicrous claims about private individuals on matters of public concern may nonetheless be protected speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such statements often fall within protected categories, agencies should hesitate before removing them merely for offensiveness; context and whether the statement constitutes an actionable tort (e.g., defamation with requisite falsity and fault) should guide moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability considerations and 47 U.S.C. § 230 immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 230(c)(1) states that no provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of information provided by another information content provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As users of interactive computer services, federal agencies are likely insulated from state tort liability for third-party comments under § 230, including for injunctive relief in many cases. Agencies should not allow speculative fear of tort liability to drive overbroad removal practices, though they may still choose to remove or act more swiftly where criminal conduct appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign immunity and constitutional claims (APA § 702 waiver)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is potential for a citizen to bring a First Amendment claim seeking non-monetary relief (e.g., injunction to compel posting); 5 U.S.C. § 702 contains a waiver of sovereign immunity for persons 'suffering legal wrong' from agency action, but courts debate whether comment removal counts as 'agency action' under the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuit precedent (e.g., Ninth and D.C. Circuits) suggests constitutional claims seeking non-monetary relief against agencies may proceed despite arguments about final agency action under § 704. Agencies should recognize that removing comments can give rise to constitutional litigation and that § 702 may permit suits for injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorsement and appearance of government speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern exists that leaving private speech posted on an agency site could create the appearance of governmental endorsement; conversely, recasting a site as government speech allows the agency to edit content but undermines a participatory forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid converting interactive agency sites into government speech; instead use clear disclaimers that the agency does not endorse private speech and that the site is a limited public forum. Disclaimers have been important in Establishment Clause and public-forum cases (e.g., Pinette, Rosenberger) to clarify non-endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited public forum framework as the guiding doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewing agency-sponsored social media sites as limited public fora permits those sites to function as arenas for public discourse where private speech is constitutionally protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat on-topic private speech as protected even if inane, offensive, or hateful (so long as it is topical). Purely private insults or slurs unconnected to the site's subject-matter category may be off-topic and therefore subject to removal. The limited public forum doctrine is recommended as the most suitable compass for agency social media moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual, case-by-case decisionmaking (reasoned judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no shortcut; moderation decisions must be made case-by-case, looking at the substance and context of government action or inaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should exercise reasoned and informed judgment: be more proactive in removing apparent crimes (cyberstalking, harassment), consider waiting to remove allegedly tortious comments until a complaint is received, avoid preemptive overbroad removal that chills speech, and weigh mission-based interests (e.g., public health) when deciding whether to remove falsehoods that could cause harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disclaimers and separation of official content from interactive content
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong disclaimer separating the agency’s official informational website from interactive social media sites can affect the analysis of removal decisions and reduce concerns about endorsement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should post clear disclaimers explaining that interactive comments are private speech and that the agency does not sponsor or endorse them; such disclaimers can make a governmental interest in managing misinformation (especially on mission-critical topics like public health) more persuasive and can allay endorsement concerns.
